utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to remind you where we were yesterday, we were talking about directive 7 and the words expressed within that directive, and your last -- our last question and answer, just to remind you, I asked: "My question is that you had stated there, hadn't you, that these words were very grave, yes? Very grave?" You said -- you answered: "If you allow me, those were not words, that was a written document. None of my superiors ever informed me verbally to act in that way, after all an order that I have to act upon as well as other subordinate corps commands did not receive such a task."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I would like to have up on the screen, please, P03040.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, you can see there -- you've seen this document before, it's dated the 20th of March, 1995, from the Drina Corps command and it is directed to your unit, amongst others, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, amongst others, headed, you can see the heading there: "Order for defence and active combat operations, operate number 7."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we turn in e-court, please, to page 6 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see there under the heading number 2: Tasks -- the tasks of the Drina Corps --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In English it's the preceding page, the heading.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And then if you read that first paragraph as you go through it, I'm going to take it up about four lines -- three or four lines down in the B/C/S and English and it says this "tasks for the Drina Corps" this is headed. "While in the direction" -- taking it up halfway through the sentence: "While in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing any communication between individuals in the two enclaves." And then this sentence: "By planned and well thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." So you received this order; is that correct? You can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my last testimony in the case of General Mladic, I was shown this same document and I would kindly appreciate if you can show me what I said on that occasion because I didn't listen to the tape. I'm not sure, but most probably that's what I said. That was in March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- could you repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was drafted in March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm confused why you want to look at your Mladic testimony. I'm just asking you about this document. It's addressed to your unit; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the heading you can see that it is also addressed to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you would have received it, you were the commander of the unit, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You remember these words?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. Until I have seen them in the document, I didn't remember those words.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, on the 2nd of July you had your preparatory order that we saw yesterday from the Drina Corps, and the order for Krivaja 95, the order for active combat activities. You remember receiving that order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You've looked at it on many occasions previously in these proceedings. I'm not going to show it to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And that order, it's right, isn't it, that order was also issued pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I explained yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just get the document up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: P04481, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see there the heading in your brigade as an addressee to the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, 2nd July, Krivaja 95, the order for Krivaja 95; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a task for active operations, but it is a very specific task. The previous order that you showed me a minute ago which was drafted in March was handed over to me for information only because my brigade was not holding positions or holding the lines facing the enclaves, hence, according to the March order, I was not obliged to become involved in any active operations towards the enclave. As for this order --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay, just a moment. So you're saying you didn't read the March order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I hadn't read it. I believe that it reached my unit, but since the brigade was not in combat contact with the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning the enclaves, I had no obligation to pursue active operations towards the enclaves, and therefore I did not pay attention to this specific task.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And is your evidence then that had you paid attention to this task you would have been shocked and horrified to have read the order: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that I never ever said anything in that respect, and I would like you to show me the transcript of any statement of mine and that I never said that I would be shocked. I don't use such words and I think it's necessary for you to show me the exact content of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the second paragraph, please, of this 2nd July document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: If we can look at page 3 of the English and in the B/C/S, please, at page -- similarly at page 3. Sorry, my apologies, in B/C/S it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can see the second point: "The command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone as soon as possible, in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and to reduce them to their urban areas." You can see that. And if I just take it up to paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- paragraph 4 identifies the objective: "By surprise attack, to separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." I don't want to stay too long with this document. I want to ask you the question: You would accept, would you, that this order is issued pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1 as is stated there, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you'll allow me. Yesterday I said that you are taking out of the context of the entire directive one single sentence, and it's being used in the indictments as a description of how the enclaves were treated. The entirety of directive 7 is a document drafted based on the analysis of the situation in Republika Srpska or the Serbian Republic of BH in the previous year and it reflects an attempt to find a solution in order to change the situation in compliance with the objectives set by the leadership of Republika Srpska. This directive does not have its objectives and it doesn't have any dead-lines. It was written for the year of 1995 and it was forwarded to the commands so that on the basis of these optional solutions that can produce a resolution, they would plan their activities in 1995. Hence, the first order of the Drina Corps command was written in March. As for this order and the reason underlying it is what is written under item 1, and that is this resulted from the activities to -- done by the BH army in the enclaves. As for the solutions, the corps commander is using the contents of directive 7 in order to resolve the situation in his zone, and there is under this item no reference to hopelessness of the situation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Right. I'm not asking you about this sentence for this -- this document. I'm just asking you about the plain wording of paragraph 2, but if you're not going to answer my question, perhaps we'll move on. I asked you, paragraph 2, the task there that the Drina Corps identifies is identified as pursuant to operations directive number 7 and 7/1, and you'd agree that that is what is stated there at the second point to -- there of that document, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These directives provide the rights and the authorities for operational activities to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's move on to July, 11th July. You entered Srebrenica. You met and greeted Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we can see that, Your Honours, on the Srebrenica trial video transcript, that's P04202 at page 21 and pages 201 and 202.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's right, you entered Srebrenica when you left -- July; right? We're not going to look at the stills. You can just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you make your question shorter. I was expecting to see the footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you meet and greet Mladic on the 11th of July in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into any detail. I'm going to go to the 12th of July, to the meeting, the meeting you had at night and that you have noted in your diary, 65 ter 25028. You testified previously that General Krstic was there, Drina Corps brigade commanders. You arrived around 9.00, is that right, before 9.00?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I noted in my diary is correct and I stand by it concerning the timing but also with respect to other noted situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And it's page 28 of the English and in the B/C/S also at page 28. General Mladic came at 2200 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 25028. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D3748, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: There is a meeting followed by a dinner; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you see that. I myself don't see any note to the effect that dinner followed a meeting. The meeting started at 10.00, that is to say 2200 hours, but it doesn't say that it was after dinner.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You aren't now denying that there was a dinner; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did Zvonko Bajagic at any point -- did you see him in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you remember what you ate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In your statement you say that there was no mention of killing people in Potocari, no information of any plan to execute persons from Srebrenica. Now, there's been numerous occasions on which you've testified about this meeting. I want to ask you, on this occasion do you now accept that you discussed at least the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss that. Instead, General Mladic talked to someone on the phone, an individual, concerning the logistical issues pertaining to the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, for 65 ter 25276 to be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's your testimony in the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And could we have e-court page 66.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, can we please be told to -- which date this entry refers?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, it's been agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the parties not agree that it was on 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I clarified that with the parties yesterday. Yes, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I -- if there -- if this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, for fear that there's any issue over the date, I'd like to just go back to the diary, please. It's not the D3748 portion of it so it's back to the 65 ter 25028.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And if we can just go to page 25 both of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was there an issue with regard to the order of these entries in terms of paginating.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Trivic will be able to confirm that the Srebrenica component of this diary is in the right order, going from 1 to 25 to 30 and so on. And then the diary is turned over and the Zepa component of the diary then begins flipped over and is numbered therefore out of order from page 75, I think it is, back -- back through, page 60, 50, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Is that correct, you can confirm that, Mr. Trivic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like us to keep to certain sequence. First there was mention of the meeting on the 12th at 10.00 in the staff headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade. Now I see that this is the 12th, 9.00 in the morning. Now, I would like to know to which specific part of my diary you would like to put a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just don't -- don't worry about the entry for the 12th for the time being. His Honour asked a question and I was trying to elicit clarification from you about how this diary is structured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not because of me but because Mr. Karadzic asked the date, to confirm the date of the meeting at 10.00, although he agreed that it was on the 12th. We wanted to make sure with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So we're not going to look at these meetings here, these morning meetings, but just to confirm with you that at page 25 what you see there is your diary starting for the 12th at 0900 hours, is that right, you can see circled?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And then on that page --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- you record entries which we're not going to look at for 0900 hours. And then if we go over to page 26 in both languages, there's actually another meeting there, isn't there, with General Krstic, recorded as no time at Vijogor village. We're not going to go into that but that's the sequence. It's later in the day, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And then we go through that meeting to the following page, 27, we don't need to look at that page. We go through it to page 28 of both B/C/S and English and that's sequentially, isn't it, still on the 12th of July. We then have the meeting at Bratunac Brigade headquarters and you have there the entry of General Mladic coming at 2200 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, in light of the testimony right now, we'll admit from page 25 to 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would just point out for clarification that if you just look at the very next page of this diary it starts on a meeting of the 10.00 hours on the 13th, so I think that this confirms that this all took place on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, well perhaps if we could also have admitted the following page, 29. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, we were looking at your Mladic testimony, 65 ter 25276, please, and it's page 66, just to remind you what I'd asked you a few moments ago in relation to that. I'd asked you whether you now accepted that you discussed at least the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari. And let me just remind you of your earlier testimony in the Mladic case. I'll just read from Judge Orie's question to give you context at line 6: "Judge Orie: We have now spent two or three questions on whether prisoners or personal prisoners or disarmed enemy soldiers were mentioned. Were they not mentioned at all during the meeting, in between the meetings, dinner, after dinner, before dinner? Was any -- but was it ever mentioned that there were prisoners or possibly prisoners or disarmed enemy soldiers? Clear question, please, a short answer." And your answer: "Thank you. During that day at the meeting and during the dinner there was no talk of prisoners of war or disarmed enemy forces. All that was discussed was the evacuation of the population, evacuation of the Muslim population from Potocari." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember in relation to this testimony there was a problem and then I asked that the tape be heard to check what I said. There was a certain slip of the tongue by attorney Lukic who had put a question regarding a meeting that day at the Fontana Hotel, and that's where some confusion occurred about the question. And then the Presiding Judge, in order to clarify everything at my request for the tape to be listened again, he granted a break and then after the break we did not go back, they did not take me back again to that question or to the substance of my testimony regarding that particular question. I said earlier that the only thing in my view, according to my recollection that had to do with the evacuation, was a telephone conversation by General Mladic about the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, it's right, isn't it, you did -- these words did slip out during your answer to Judge Orie's question, they slipped out, and -- and you subsequently denied having said them and the transcript was then checked. And here is the transcript, still retaining the words that you said during your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not permitted to put any questions then and to respond to a specific question in order to clarify the situation. They said that that matter was done. I don't want you to use something that I was not permitted to express my view once more about that particular meeting at the brigade HQ.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you were given an opportunity, Colonel Trivic, and the point is that those words inadvertently slipped out in your answer to a question from the Judge and they, in fact, expressed the truth of the matter, don't they, that that was a topic that was discussed at that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the topic that was discussed at that meeting, and I repeat, I said then also - I even told the Presiding Judge or his associate - that I did not permit anyone to impute to me something that I never said. I did not say that the topic of the meeting was the evacuation of the population, but the report and tasks for the continuing activities by the army. Perhaps this was discussed at some other meeting, but I did not attend any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to move on to the 13th of July. You testified previously about leaving then towards Zepa and passing Nova Kasaba. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to 65 ter 25032.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is your testimony in the Popovic case, and I'd like to turn, please, to e-court page 65. And it's taking it up from the bottom of the page and then we are going to go over to pages 66 and 67 and I will read it slowly. And I'm going to read this testimony to you and I'm going to ask you if you confirm it, please. Just to put it in the context, you were talking about your journey passed -- your route passed Nova Kasaba at around 1700 hours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're talking about your journey at around 1700 hours when you passed Nova Kasaba, is that right? You remember the timing being around 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was recorded, I don't know and it says here 11, but I think it was in the afternoon. But I accept this as the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I do accept the testimony as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. So just taking it up then. The question: "And en route to Krivaca, did you see any groups of Muslim prisoners anywhere?" Your answer: "Yes, of course. I saw a large group of people sitting down on the football-pitch in a settlement called Nova Kasaba, on the right-hand side of the road as I was moving."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: If we could go to page 66, please: "And do you recall how those prisoners were arranged, if at all, on that football field, in what manner, if at all? "A. They sat in rows. "Q. And can you estimate at all, approximately, how many prisoners you saw on that football field as you drove by? "A. Earlier in my testimony -- it's difficult to give an evaluation knowing the size of the football-pitch and the markings on the pitch. It's difficult to evaluate how many people can be seated on 100 square metre. Well, if you manage to estimate that number, you can multiply it by 100. I never tried before to arrive at a number. If you can seat two people on one square metre, then you can possibly calculate how many there were. "Q. Well, let me ask you this, then, sir: Do you recall approximately how full this football field was with prisoners? "A. That entire area was covered with people sitting. "Q. And who was guarding them? "A. I was able to see military policemen, and I believe there were soldiers, conscripts doing their regular military service and who were in training in Nova Kasaba, which had a military police battalion that trained these soldiers; that is, younger soldiers who were in training to become military policemen. I don't know. Maybe there were some senior troops as well, but I remember the younger ones. "Q. And to which unit was this military police battalion attached, sir? "A. It belonged to the Protection Regiment of the Main Staff." Over on to the following page, please: "Q. Is that also known as the 65th Protection Regiment, sir? "A. Yes. "Q. And are you aware of whether or not there is a facility for that military police battalion in that area? "A. That military police battalion was normally stationed in that area, in that settlement, in the school building, and this site was just outside the settlement. The football-pitch was just outside the settlement where those seated people were." And just taking it up from lower down the page: "Q. And during this period of time, in July of 1995, did you know any of the officers within the 65th Protection Regiment or the military police battalion of that regiment personally; and if you did, can you tell the Trial Chamber their names and position? "A. I certainly knew the regiment commander, Colonel Savcic, and I also knew Major Malinic, who was the commander of that battalion in Nova Kasaba, the battalion that had those young soldiers in training."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you testified to that effect in the Mladic -- sorry, in the Popovic case, and you would confirm the truth of your testimony in -- would you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And if we can just go to 65 ter 25276 at page 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We're going back to the Mladic testimony now, talking further about the football-pitch at the top of page 80 and you're asked -- you answer: "They said at the football-pitch, at the football stadium, on the right side of the road as I was moving along the road, I cannot tell you how many there were. I didn't count. But almost the entire football-pitch was taken up by them. They sat on that pitch." And the Judge asked you: "How were they dressed?" You answer: "They were in the clothes that they wore at the time. I didn't pay attention to what they were wearing. This was in Nova Kasaba. Along the road I saw several smaller groups of disarmed --" And the Judge asks you: "I am asking about Nova Kasaba. You explained that you saw them sitting on the football-pitch, and were they in uniforms or in civilian clothes? "A. I didn't pay attention to the clothes that they wore. I don't think it's important. They could have changed their clothes to fair better." You stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And let me please ask you about a further passage of testimony in the Mladic, and this is just moving back, I'm afraid, to page 77. This was in answer to questions from Judge Orie. Now, you have clarified in your prior testimony - this was in Popovic prior to this - you clarified that you regarded these men, these men you saw in Nova Kasaba sitting in rows on the football-pitch as "disarmed enemy forces," not detainees. Would you stand by that prior testimony, that was how you characterised these men?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And so you're asked -- I just remind you of your testimony in Mladic regarding this at page 77. And you were asked by Judge Orie: "Sill, my question is: How could you know that they were -- and for example, not non-combatants? "A. All of them who had set out to break through towards Tuzla, towards the canton where they wanted to go, in order not to become prisoners of war, all of them put themselves in the position of being disarmed enemy forces. "Q. So therefore your explanation is that if someone decided to try to leave the area through the woods instead of surrendering, that they for that reason were part of enemy forces. Is that your testimony? "A. All of those who decided to set out with the soldiers of the 28th Division - I don't know whether all of them were members of the 28th Division or not, nobody knows that - but all of those who had set out to break through expecting to go towards their own free territory across the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska brought themselves in a position where they became disarmed enemy forces because the Army of Republika Srpska was concluding its offensive and was in the pursuit stage. Had they decided earlier on to surrender via their representatives, via their commanders, once they saw that they were in an impossible situation, then they would have become prisoners of war. This was my interpretation and the interpretation of the international laws of war." You go on: "They put themselves in this situation where they became disarmed enemy forces." You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the testimony, but there is something in the translation that in another situation or during deliberations of charges in the indictment, I did not say that the Army of Republika Srpska was concluding the offensive or was in the pursuit stage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Trivic, the interpreters missed part of your answer. Could you repeat it, kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the gist, and of course I would repeat the same thing, perhaps not word for word the way it was said then. But there is one problem in the interpretation, at least that's how I heard it. In the part which says that the Army of Republika Srpska was in the pursuit stage, you cannot translate it like that, "u fazi progona." I don't know English, so perhaps you can look at that and correct it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your qualification of -- of these men whom you saw sitting in Nova Kasaba at the football field. Can I pursue it --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- you accept, don't you, that the group you saw at Nova Kasaba included civilians, but your point is that they brought themselves into the position where they became disarmed enemy soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, you're aware now that many hundreds of Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can intervene. I'm interested in hearing from the witness about his explanation about pursuit stage. Could you explain it to me so that I can understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It was said but it didn't -- hadn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'm asking the witness to explain to us in simple terms so that we can understand him well. It was recorded that "the Army of Republika Srpska was concluding its offensive and was in the pursuit stage." Could you tell us what it meant or how it should have been reflected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part that was read out to me right now, Mr. President, is correct. During an offensive, an assault, which the Army of Republika Srpska or the Drina Corps was in the process of executing at -- during those days consists of three phases. There is contact with enemy forces, contact and decisive battle, that's the second phase. And the last phase is pursuit of those who can no longer put up resistance but do not wish to surrender. That is the third phase of an offensive according to the rules on offensive action of the then-JNA of the former state which would end with the phase that is referred to as pursuit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're aware now, aren't you, that many hundreds of the men held at Nova Kasaba were subsequently executed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if those men were executed, the men that I saw as I was passing by, the men that were standing at that football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, you said they were sitting in rows?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could see they were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: They were, weren't they, under armed guard with soldiers with guns pointed at them, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were guarded by soldiers, soldiers at the time when the state of war or imminent danger of war was declared. They had weapons and those who were executing their guard duties also around the football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you avoid qualifying them as detainees; rather, you describe them as disarmed enemy soldiers. Why? Why don't you call them detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the enemy side, the opposing side, in an offensive is defeated and does not accept that defeat correctly but tries to break through to part of its own free territory, and then it gets to the stage where it is disarmed by the strength of the force that defeated it, then that group of people brings itself in the situation of being a disarmed enemy force. And the -- and instead of acknowledging that they were defeated, they would become --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, could you repeat from where you said that group of people brings itself in the situation of being a disarmed enemy force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The commanders, komandirs and commandants who evaluate that they can no longer put up any resistance or for any other reason, they did not accept to acknowledge their defeat and to surrender and to be listed by the enemy, but instead decided to go and attempt a break through to their free territory. That phase of pursuit led to them being intercepted, prevented from reaching the free territory, and they were then disarmed. But still, at that point in time they have not become prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So put simply then, is it okay to kill them all, those who were sitting at the football-pitch, because they were not prisoners of war? Is that your evidence, Mr. Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never said that, and in any case I do not approve of something like that. But that is not my testimony, that then it is all right to treat them however anyone wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm aware of the time. I'll just be another five minutes or so, just another entry of the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to move on from this topic. I'd like to take you, please, to your diary again back --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And it's the entry on the 16th of July. This is then going from the back of the diary non-sequentially. I would like to take you to page 73 which is the first day entry for the 16th of July, just to confirm we've got the right date. I'm not going to ask you about what you detailed there, but this is just to have you confirm that we are looking at your entry dated 16 July, 2000 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This was at a time when you were engaged in the Zepa operation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let us go, please, to page 72, which would be the next recorded entry in your diary for the 16th of July. This is in B/C/S and English. And you record there a meeting with General Krstic on the 16th of July, yes? Let me just read that out and just refresh your memory of the content. The first point, this is General Krstic presumably speaking to you, addressing you: "The VRS Supreme Command has decided that eastern parts of Republika Srpska must be liberated from the Turks." Do you remember him telling you that, "the Supreme Command has decided the eastern parts of RS must be liberated from the Turks "?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he said that. I wrote that down and I explained that to Mr. McCloskey, this expression, "Turks," as we soldiers called each other. They called Serbs Chetniks and we called them Turks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The second point: "The brilliant victory in Srebrenica is the biggest boost in morale ." Then there's point 3: "The situation in the Srebrenica - Birac enclave," two points: "Small groups of civilians. "Small armed groups." So there you separate civilians from the armed groups?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You understand that distinction; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And then you go on to further state: "The 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade and the 1st Bratunac Brigade - to search the terrain. "4. The situation in the zone of responsibility of the ... Zvornik Infantry Brigade is very complex." And then I'd ask that we go to page 71, the next part of the entry: "Part of the Muslim's 28th Division has crossed the /canyon?/ Karakaj - Crni Vrh and reached the Bajkovica sector (around 2.000 soldiers)." So those are the entries, what you were told by Krstic at that meeting on the 16th of July; is that right? You go on further but I'm not going to go through that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a correction, it's not a canyon, I want to correct that. The interpretation was part of the 28th Division has crossed the canyon, not the canyon but the road Karakaj-Crni Vrh, it is "komunikacija" not "kanjon." I would like that to be corrected. Karakaj-Crni Vrh and reached Bajkovica sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. If we go to page 70 and this is the following part of your entry for 16th July. You talk about: "Must enter Zepa by 1400 hours tomorrow." Then you have an entry: "PAD for launching aerial bombs to come tomorrow ..." I just want to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I have one clarification, whether those words are of the witness or he wrote -- recorded somebody else's words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can take up that issue in your re-examination. Yes, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We're dealing with the PAD for launching aerial bombs, and you talked about this -- you'd been asked to describe what this entry pertains to in your earlier testimony. I'll ask to look at the Tolimir testimony at 65 ter 25033 at page 72. My apologies, I didn't ask, but with the diary I'd ask to have admitted those pages related to the 16th July. What -- we'll be looking at them again after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just for now. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add them to the Exhibit P3748.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And let me just read that out for your benefit. You just describe what this entry pertains to: "A. This entry pertains to the task to launch from an improvised launch pad on a vehicle, launching of an aerial bomb which could not be launched in the standard way but was, rather, used to produce psychological effects in a larger area, to affect the attitude of the people, not because it had chemical effects or anything of the sort but, rather, because it was supposed to produce a large explosion. It was supposed to be launched from a trailer. Its popular name was sow, 'krmaca' in Serbian. That's what this aerial bomb was called but it wasn't really very accurate." You stand by that prior testimony, would you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in the original part there's something wrong with the interpretation. It's not improvised, it's the launching pad that's improvised on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the translation didn't get to you properly. What I read was this entry pertains to the task to launch from an improvised launch pad on a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This answer of mine has to do with a question and an explanation as to what this pad is, but there was no reference to whether there had been any firing. I was explaining what the effects were of that bomb, what effects are achieved when it is launched, and it is not directly related to what I noted down on the 16th. Over there, it just says that that launching pad is supposed to get somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was just one matter because the witness had asked a question about whether or not he had heard back from the Chamber regarding his query over the transcript in Mladic. This was a topic I discussed earlier. And I have the entry and I just wanted to at least for the witness's benefit just go back and show him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- the matter had been readdressed. So we can just go back, please, to the Mladic transcript which is 25276.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just to -- page 86 of that transcript. So just -- just to read what you were informed of then by Judge Orie. This was on the second day of your testimony you were told: "Before Mr. Lukic continues his cross-examination, I would briefly like to deal with a matter which arose yesterday. On the record we saw that you had referred to the evacuation of the Muslim population from Potocari and a few minutes later you denied to have said any of such thing, and I even suggested to you that you might consider that you may have said it but that -- that you do not exclude for that possibility. You insisted on it being verified. It has been verified. That means the audio has been listened to and the translation has been verified. This is what you said: "'Thank you. During that day at the meeting and during the dinner, there was no talk of prisoners of war or disarmed enemy forces. All that was discussed was the evacuation of the population, evacuation of the Muslim population from Potocari.'" The Judge continues: "This is what you said and that was how it was translated to us." Okay?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, but then just this connection with that telephone conversation that General Mladic had, not with us, the persons attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's not what you say, is it? And I would suggest to you that those words slipped out because you did discuss this topic and you unfortunately hurried then to retract; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness said it was out of confusion. Shall we leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little bit, I hope, not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, good day.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your diary the last entry for the month of July is the 29th of July. Can you tell us whether at any one of these meetings anyone mentioned killing of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at a single one of these meetings, those that have been recorded and also those possible contacts that I had with certain persons at that time. There was no talk of any killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 25, line 16, it says the Prosecutor says then you say whose words did you write down in your diary, your own or somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attending meetings at one's superior means that one should record what the superior officer is conveying. That is how it is in military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 16 and 17 you said that prisoners of war sat in an area of about 100 square metres, and if two persons were sitting in one square metre that that would have to be multiplied. What are the dimensions of the sides of this rectangle or square of 100 square metres?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert. I was surprised by that question then as to how many persons that would entail in such an area, a pitch. I did not really think about how many people could sit in a football-pitch. Dimensions vary, I assume, they vary. An Olympic stadium is not the same size as a village stadium and so on. So I wouldn't want to speculate with numbers. Obviously this 100 square metres is 10 by 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 65 ter 2841.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, if you wrote down in your diary who was present, would you write down when people would leave early?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did that. I'm almost sure I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now zoom in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, take a look at this. Are you familiar with this image, the 13th of July at 2.00 p.m., is that the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now enlarge the stadium itself, please. A little bit more if possible, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the image that you saw as you passed by the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is an image -- actually, this is the first time I see this, so it jogs my memory, the first time since I passed there. And this commotion along the road, that involved those who were security people and then there were journalists and cameramen and some other soldiers. So now this reminds me. So it's not only trees. I assume that this is satellite imagery and it involves persons who were also standing by the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this rectangle, Colonel, do you see these shadows, these figures, the four in front of them, are those the guards? And did they hold these people at gunpoint, these people who were sitting there, as had been suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at any point in time, not here and also not the other groups that I saw along the road. There were soldiers who were guarding these persons, that was the order of the command of the Drina Corps, to guard these possible POWs. So they were not holding them at gunpoint. They were guarding them like any soldier would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that this has already been admitted and that it does have an exhibit number, a P number; if not, I would be happy to have it signed and admitted. But I believe it's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I cannot help you in this regard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going to say I'm sure it's admitted. I don't know the number offhand. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so there's no doubt about the reference, I think we should just admit this as a separate exhibit so that we know which photo this witness was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if it turned out that it has already been admitted, we can strike it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, it's at page 27 of the Jean-Rene Ruez book of photographs, but I don't have -- I unfortunately I don't have the exhibit number on me right now -- perhaps not page 27, sorry. The one that's been referred to is page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's admit it temporarily.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3749, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, on page 6 something was discussed. You said that directive 7 and directive 7/1 was used as a basis which gave the commander the right to act further. Could you tell us whether everything from the directive has to be carried out? Actually, to what extent can a commander be creative, or rather, assess the situation as it is? In addition to exercising that right, does he have to check everything?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the answer I've already provided today to one of the questions, I said that a directive is a document, is written on the basis of an analysis of the situation in the previous period. In this situation, I think that it was written after the analysis of the situation in 1994 and that is why it was passed sometime in May for 1995. So it had to do with analysing the situation, seeing how objectives should be attained as the struggle for exercising the rights of the Serbs as a constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina started. So all of these problems were looked at and then it was put on paper according to regions in Republika Srpska that were covered by different corps of the Army of Republika Srpska, which activities, which tasks, how they will act in order to improve or at least maintain the situation as it was. The Drina Corps was rather specific and it had this problem too, protection from enclaves. So they had a territory that had temporarily been taken up of its own area of defence. So that corps commander or the commander of the Drina Corps did not -- actually, just used those rights in terms of being able to act to improve his position, and he also asked for what he could do on the basis of his own assessment. In this situation it was that action with the part of the free forces of the Drina Corps to make the enclaves narrower, to separate them, and to prevent further terror from the enclaves, by engaging also part of the 2nd Romanija Brigade which did not have positions facing the enclaves, but had the task as a subordinate unit to send part of its forces to join those forces that were supposed to carry out that offensive in terms of improving the position of that unit in its own area of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. On page 5 what was read out to you was an order and it said: "Create conditions for resolving or eliminating or liquidating enclaves." What does this term mean, "create conditions"? Can that be done without a new order or does any creation of conditions have to be taken into account as something that will actually be carried through? What does it mean actually?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that that's from the order for action, where the objective of the forces involved in Krivaja 95 is to narrow down the enclaves and to create conditions. So the objective ends with the separation and creating conditions for some further orders, assessments, and so on, whether it is possible, whether it's not possible, but to bring them into the situation so that they can take a further activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This new activity, can it be carried out without a new order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, no, but except in situations when conditions are altered in the course of carrying out an activity in order to achieve a certain objective. In this particular instance it meant amending the initial order that had to be amended because you have to create conditions to have the axis of operations moved closer to Srebrenica because we had daily assessments of the results achieved and then the following day we adjusted the axis of operation towards the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4 it was suggested to you that you had stated that you were shocked and then you corrected that. Can you tell us, would you have carried out the element in the directive that did not feature in the order? Did you -- would you have carried it out had it been included in the order and would any commander be obliged to carry out something that would constitute a crime?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no contents of that nature that was conveyed to me as a commander, either verbally or orally; and if it had been the case, I wouldn't have carried it out and I'm quite sure that none of my colleagues, other commanders, would carry out something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Thank you for coming here and answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted down on my book and I forgot that Jean-Rene Ruez's book was admitted in its entirety as Exhibit P4308.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, and -- and, Mr. President, this -- this document that is referred to is at page 36 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Trivic. On behalf of the Chamber I'd like to thank you for you coming to The Hague to give it yet again. Now you are free to go, but let us rise all together. The Chamber will have a break for 20 minutes and we'll have another break during the course of next witness's evidence. We'll resume at 11.00 -- oh, I'm sorry, we'll resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karisik. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Karisik, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Karisik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must ask you - and I will do as well - to pause between questions and answers and to speak slowly so that everything that we say can be interpreted and recorded in the transcript. General, have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read a summary of General Milenko Karisik's statement in English. [In English] General Milenko Karisik was in a special unit of the BH MUP from 1983 until the outbreak of the war. He served as deputy commander of the special anti-terrorist unit of the BH MUP. This unit was the strike force of the MUP of BH. The strict regime for using this unit required legal and professional justification for performance of the most difficult tasks. Special attention was paid to ensure that the staffing structure corresponded to the population of BH. After the multi-party elections in BH in 1990, the SDA personnel were appointed to key supervisory positions in the Ministry of Internal Affairs of BH. This undermined the legality of the work and professional principles of the organs of the ministry. A new organisation of the MUP was imposed. The number of active policemen was increased and, in particular, the reserve forces, mostly Muslims, were activated in all organs at all levels. Huge resources were invested to arm the Muslims and Croats for conflict to create a unitary BH to the detriment of the Serbs. Particular problems appeared in late 1991 because of the negative tendencies in the MUP headquarters. The unit started to perform tasks that were not within its remit. Anti-terrorism training transitioned to military training. There was clear deviation from the regular training plan in preparation for new purposes. After the unit was compromised in this way, mixed motorised patrols were set up with members of the special unit and members of the JNA. They did not defuse tensions on the ground but provoked adverse reactions. At one meeting, Mr. Cengic said, quoting: "The Muslims will sacrifice a million people for a sovereign Bosnia." The special reserve unit was filled only with Muslims. The formation of this armed unit undermined the ethnic mix to the benefit of the Muslims. Muslim officers who deserted the ranks of the JNA were appointed to commanding positions already held by officers from the professional special unit. The personnel service of the MUP of BH was completely gripped by lawless behaviour, upsetting the ethnic mix of the unit. Recruitment was carried out without any regard to selection criteria. After a series of the abuses in the use of the unit, Serbian professional specials reacted by demanding a meeting with the MUP leadership. Although agreement was reached, it was not respected and the unit was misused again on orders from the Muslim representatives. This impacted on the internal unity of the unit, and led to the breakdown of personal relationships and trust. After the failed attempts to keel life and work in the unit within the framework of valid legal regulations of the MUP, working together became impossible. Momcilo Mandic signed a dispatch to split the MUP on 4th of April, 1992. Based on the agreement reached at the top of MUP, the bases in Vraca, in the MUP school, went to the Serbian part, and Muslim-Croatian part of the specials remained in Krtelji. It was agreed that the Serbian specials would leave with their personal weapons, equipment, and vehicles, but without armoured personnel carriers. Milenko Karisik and his unit entered the school centre and encountered an unexpected problem, coming under cross-fire from two directions from Muslim paramilitary formations. They were forced to defend themselves. Two Serbs were killed and another seriously injured; however, none of the Muslims or Croats were hurt because the Serbs' intention was only to save their lives. The Muslim MUP leadership had ordered the director of the school centre not to allow Serbian specials to enter their base and to use an armed operation to prevent it, the implementation of the agreement on the splitting up of the special unit. For the Muslim side, this conflict was a test of the functioning of its paramilitary police organisation which they had been preparing for a long time. They wanted to determine the readiness to use force and war to determine their destiny and the Serbs. The special units remained in Vraca until 10th of June, 1992. From late July 1992 onwards, the detachment was located in Zvornik. While in Vraca they came under daily attacks from Muslim forces. They were attacked by infantry and anti-armour weapons and mortars as well as other artillery weapons. General Milenko Karisik had no contacts with the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo. No non-Serbs were forcibly driven out of Vraca and Grbavica. By mid-1992, the unit operated together with the Territorial Defence in Sarajevo in the defence and protection of the Serbs and Serbian settlements. From mid-May 1992, the unit co-ordinated actions within the VRS. After three months of engagement in Sarajevo, Milenko Karisik's unit was engaged in combat tasks throughout Republika Srpska. The unit did not mount offensive operations, but engaged in ad hoc combat operation zones if lines of combat were breached and civilian population endangered. The unit was used to disarm paramilitary units appearing on the Serb side in Republika Srpska. The unit also took measures to establish law and order in Republika Srpska, and to prevent serious crimes. General Milenko Karisik's unit acted in line with the rules of service and rules of war, as well as the Geneva Conventions. It never committed a single crime. General Karisik was commander of the special police brigade until February 1994, when he moved to the chief of the police administration. In November 1994, he was appointed deputy minister of the interior and chief of the RJB, public security department. No one informed Milenko Karisik that any crimes had been committed against the Muslims in Srebrenica. There were no plans to expel civilians forcibly from Srebrenica or plans to capture and liquidate members of the 28th Muslim Division -- Division of Muslim army. Milenko Karisik was not a member of the SDS or any other political party. He never received instructions from them on any basis for the conduct of action of his unit. The unit never committed a crime against Muslims or Croats. No one ever asked him to commit a war crime. He never received any kind of order directly from Radovan Karadzic. General Milenko Karisik never informed President Karadzic orally or in writing that prisoners from Srebrenica had been executed. He didn't have that information himself. And that would be the summary. At that moment I do not have questions for General Karisik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that Defence is not tendering any of the associated exhibits admission of which was denied?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before we hear the cross. Mr. Karadzic called you -- addressed you as "General." Could you tell us why it was so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, in 1993 or 1994, I cannot remember exactly, received the rank of general. I got the rank because I was the commander of that unit and the president himself perhaps can explain better himself why I was given the rank of general. As a professional staff member of the MUP, I followed that line. I successfully formed the special police in detachment form. Later it was turned into the special brigade, and because the unit waged war honourably to the extent that it was involved in combat operations and because I saved many Serbian civilians because many times lines were broken and it was a bad situation at the front and in essence we tried, even though as a mobile unit, we tried to defensively protect our population. And in any event, I'm sure that the decree by the president and the awarding of the rank of general is something that the president himself be better asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I forgot that the police had adopted the rank system similar to the military. That was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karisik, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before he starts his cross-examination, in terms of today's scheduling, we'll have a short break until 11.30, and we'll resume again for an hour and we'll have another lunch break. I was told that Mr. Karisik wants the session not to last more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, we're breaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And resuming at 11.30. --- Break taken at 11.17 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you're a career professional policeman before your retirement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's in your statement. And you rose really to the very top ranks of the RS MUP by July 1995, correct, just under Tomo Kovac and the minister?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: You could say that. I was the commander of the special brigade, briefly I was chief of the police administration. After that, from November 1994, I was the chief of the public security department or assistant minister of the MUP, and towards the end of my police career I was deputy minister of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And when was that, the end of your police career? When did you retire from the police?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: I retired in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And in your statement at paragraph 6 - you don't need to read it - talking about the special unit before the war, you talk about how it was comprised of outstanding professionals. So you're an outstanding professional too; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So what we have in front of us today is basically the finest of the finest of law enforcement of the RS, one of the top; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Highly trained, promoted to general; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Tomo Kovac, he's a professional too, isn't he, a good policeman?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Dragomir Vasic, also a superb professional, a good cop?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: I can confirm that, but he came to the MUP during the war. He was not a policeman before the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You answered the question --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: -- as Kovac and I were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You actually answered the question in the first four words, so you can confirm that, so that you don't always need to go beyond my questions. And what about Mane Djuric, as far as you know him, good policeman? I'm talking about the Mane Djuric who was Vasic's deputy in the Zvornik CJB in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Mane was the deputy and the best evaluation of him could be given by Vasic, who was his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I'm asking for your evaluation. If you know, do you consider him a good policeman?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And we just heard from Mr. Karadzic in his summary that your job and the job of the MUP was to establish law and order and prevent serious crime. That is the job of law enforcement; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Is the job of the MUP, what Mr. Karadzic read out in his summary, to prevent serious crime? Is that a tricky question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: The MUP is obliged to prevent crime and that is part of its remit in the territory outside of combat actions. Our territory was limited or the boundaries were the lines of separation which were held by soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska. That was no longer under the responsibility of the MUP; that was the responsibility of the army. The Ministry of the Interior outside of the separation zone and the combat operations zone was obliged to carry out its constitutional and legal duty of securing law and order, preventing all forms of crime, and so on and so forth. That is part of the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior according to the constitution and the law, securing the territory within our area of responsibility. It is not the responsibility of MUP to do that within the combat zone; that was the responsibility of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And we'll get to that and I see where you're going, but we'll get to that and flesh that out. When it's not possible to prevent serious crime or any crime and crimes have occurred, it's the job of the MUP to investigate the crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: My answer is the same here as well. The Ministry of Internal Affairs --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: -- once it finds out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you. We don't need to go into the army's job now or where the limitations of your jurisdiction are. Is the job of the MUP to investigate crimes which have occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: I was going to say that. The MUP cannot investigate crimes that occur during military operations and which are under the jurisdiction of military courts and military prosecution offices. That is something that the MUP cannot do. The MUP can investigate crimes that happened outside of the territories where the army's operating. Once they found out -- find out about it either through the police or a citizen, that when -- once they find out about it, they can initiate the regular investigative procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And so that is the job of you highly professional RS policemen, to investigate serious crimes and bring, when you can in your jurisdiction, the perpetrators to justice; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: You must repeat your question, please. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you don't understand that question, I'll just move on. Let me ask you about one part of your statement, this is paragraph 40. You're speaking about the 16th of July, 1995, and you say: "That day no one informed me in any way that any crime had been committed against the Muslims in Srebrenica." Then we switch to the present tense. So this is now, this is when you signed this statement: "I also have absolutely no knowledge of any plan to expel civilians forcibly from Srebrenica and," again present tense, "I am not aware that there was a plan to capture and liquidate members of the 28th Muslim Division." So is your honest, truthful testimony that you - one of the highest-ranking and successful law enforcement officers in the MUP who is head of the RJB in July 1995 - in 2013 are not aware that there was a plan to capture and liquidate Muslim soldiers in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I really don't know. To this day from the aspect of the clerk's duties that I was carrying out or civil servants, I was not informed by the centre of the public security station either verbally or in writing in any way that any crime had occurred --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to cut you off but you already answered the question, as you sit here today you don't know of any plan. Now, let's break that sentence down a bit. Forget the plan --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did not know. Yes, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. There was a corps of the VRS called the Drina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. As you sit here today in 2013, when you signed this statement, when you signed this statement, were you aware that after 14 July 1995 in Zvornik municipality the Drina Corps executed captured Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: All of this that you are asking me is something that I heard from the daily information media and TV news reports. I have just found out and I as a senior-ranking professional MUP officer to this very day am not quite clear about things because there is a lot of manipulation regarding the true extent, the numbers, and so on and so forth. I did not take part in that military operation, as the operation in Srebrenica was called. I was then a civil servant at the Ministry of Internal Affairs who had to carry out other assignments under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, I'm going to stop you now. I understand you keep saying how you weren't involved in the army. I understand and we'll keep going through that. Now please answer the question. In 2013, when you signed this statement, were you aware that the Drina Corps in the Zvornik municipality executed Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was answered and I have an intervention in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that can be asked again. Fair enough. Can you answer the question, Mr. Karisik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not find out. To this very day I don't know the actual truth of the true extent of the crime, the true facts. There is a lot of manipulation in the media about this, so if anybody in the world were to ask me today about exactly what happened, I would not be able to say so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript. The witness said, "and about the true nature of that crime," and that was not recorded that he said that he did not know about the extent, the number, and the nature of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do we agree there was a crime, the Muslim prisoners were executed by the Drina Corps in Zvornik after 14 July? Forget the extent or numbers, precise numbers. Do you agree that you as top MUP official know there was a crime?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO KARISIK
utterances.text: I don't know who were the perpetrators of the crime, whether they were from the Drina Corps within the military operation.
